title: What If You Went to Space WITHOUT a Suit? (Second by Second)
description:
What if you went to space without a suit? Second by second, here's what your body would do... and how long a rescue has.

Breathe out with him, touch your tongue to your lip, pinch the back of your hand, hold out your palm: four tests you can do right now, sitting down. You don't explode and you don't freeze: your spit boils at body temperature, the oxygen pours out of your blood the wrong way, and the lights go out at about fifteen seconds. Tongue, pinch or palm: which test got you?

Joe Kittinger's hand swelled to twice its size nineteen miles up in 1960. Jim LeBlanc's last memory in a NASA vacuum chamber in 1966 was the spit bubbling on his tongue. The 1960s tests found a window of about ninety seconds. A short animated film, made entirely in code. Next week: what happens if you stop brushing your teeth.

0:00 Space, no suit: breathe OUT
0:34 Second 1: do you explode?
1:00 Second 5: your spit boils
1:18 Second 10: the oxygen leaves
1:40 Second 15: lights out, the race
2:30 Second 30: the man who lived it
3:04 Second 60: how long a rescue has
3:35 Second 80: REPRESS

Sources:
Billings, "Barometric Pressure", NASA Bioastronautics Data Book, SP-3006 (1973)
Roth, NASA CR-1223 (1968): the 1966 LeBlanc accident
Bancroft & Dunn, Aerospace Medicine 36:720 (1965): dogs in near-vacuum
Koestler (ed.), NASA CR-329 (1965) and ARL-TR-67-2 (1967): chimpanzees in near-vacuum
NASA SP-4209: Soyuz 11
